section.title: Divorce, Children, and the Rich Young Man
section.sectionRationale: On the road toward Jerusalem, Jesus fields a test about divorce and recalls marriage to God's creation design. He welcomes the children the disciples would turn away, and He meets a rich young man whose wealth keeps him from the kingdom, teaching that salvation is impossible for man but possible with God.
section.thesis: The kingdom belongs to those who receive it like little children and cannot be entered by human achievement or wealth; God's design for marriage is lifelong union, and only God can save, richly rewarding all who leave everything to follow Jesus.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the question about divorce and God's design for marriage; Jesus blessing the little children; the rich young man who goes away sorrowful; and the danger of riches with the promise of reward for those who follow.

verses.text: When Jesus had finished saying these things, He left Galilee and went into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan.
Large crowds followed Him, and He healed them there.
Then some Pharisees came and tested Him by asking, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?”
Jesus answered, “Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator ‘made them male and female,’
and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’?
So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.”
“Why then,” they asked, “did Moses order a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away?”
Jesus replied, “Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart. But it was not this way from the beginning.
Now I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except for {{porneia|sexual immorality}}, and marries another woman commits adultery.”
His disciples said to Him, “If this is the case between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.”
“Not everyone can accept this word,” He replied, “but only those to whom it has been given.

For there are eunuchs who were born that way; others were made that way by men; and still others live like eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. The one who can accept this should accept it.”
Then little children were brought to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them and pray for them. And the disciples rebuked those who brought them.
But Jesus said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.”
And after He had placed His hands on them, He went on from there.
Just then a man came up to Jesus and inquired, “Teacher, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?”
“Why do you ask Me about what is good?” Jesus replied. “There is only One who is good. If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.”
“Which ones?” the man asked. Jesus answered, “‘Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness,
honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself.’”
“All these I have kept,” said the young man. “What do I still lack?”
Jesus told him, “If you want to be {{teleios|perfect}}, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.”
When the young man heard this, he went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth.

units.label: Riches, and reward for the last
units.note: impossible for man, possible with God

verses.text: Then Jesus said to His disciples, “Truly I tell you, it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.
Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.”
When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished and asked, “Who then can be saved?”
Jesus looked at them and said, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
“Look,” Peter replied, “we have left everything to follow You. What then will there be for us?”

Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, in the {{palingenesia|renewal}} of all things, when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne, you who have followed Me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for the sake of My name will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life.
But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.

porneia.gloss: Sexual immorality, unfaithfulness of a broad kind. It is the exception clause in Jesus' teaching on divorce; its precise scope is debated, but it names a grave sexual breach of the one-flesh union that Jesus alone allows as a ground for divorce.

teleios.gloss: Complete, whole, mature, perfect. Jesus tells the young man that being teleios is not another achievement to add but the surrender of the one idol, his wealth, that his heart truly serves; wholeness is found in following Christ, not in self-made righteousness.

palingenesia.gloss: Rebirth, regeneration, the renewal of all things. It names the coming restoration of creation when the Son of Man reigns on His glorious throne, the age in which Christ's followers share His reward.

basic.context: Heading toward Jerusalem, Jesus is tested about divorce. He goes back to creation: God made marriage a lifelong one-flesh union, and Moses' permission to divorce was a concession to hard hearts. He welcomes little children when the disciples try to keep them away, saying the kingdom belongs to such. A rich young man asks how to gain eternal life; when Jesus tells him to sell all and follow, he leaves grieving. Jesus warns how hard riches make entry, but with God even that is possible, and He promises great reward to those who leave all to follow Him.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the three scenes together: they all expose what we cling to instead of the kingdom, whether a lax view of marriage, adult self-importance, or wealth. Jesus grounds marriage in creation, not merely in law. The rich man's story is not a general command to sell everything but a probe of the heart's true master. Salvation, Jesus says, is God's impossible-for-man work.
basic.originalLanguages: The debated exception clause turns on porneia, sexual immorality. Jesus tells the young man that to be teleios, whole, he must give up his idol and follow. And He promises reward in the palingenesia, the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man reigns.
basic.typology: Jesus recalling the creation of marriage points to the ultimate marriage, Christ and His church. The renewal of all things fulfills the prophetic hope of a restored creation under the reign of the Son of Man.
basic.christ: Jesus speaks with the Creator's authority over marriage, welcomes the little and the least, and exposes every rival to Himself in the human heart. He is the good treasure worth more than all wealth, the one worth leaving everything to follow, and the King who will reign in the renewed world.
basic.god: God is the author of marriage, the welcomer of children, the only One who is good, and the only One who can save. What is impossible for people, He makes possible, and He richly rewards those who forsake all for His name.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 1 and 2 give the creation of marriage Jesus cites. Malachi 2 declares God hates divorce. Mark 10 and Luke 18 parallel these scenes. Revelation 21 depicts the renewal of all things Jesus promises.
basic.oneStory: As Jesus nears Jerusalem, He calls people to receive the kingdom as helpless children and to release every idol, marriage held cheap, self-importance, and wealth, that competes with God. Salvation is impossible for man but possible with God, and those who leave all to follow the King will share His reign in the renewed world. The road to the cross is the road that gains everything.

context.literary:
Matthew 19 opens with the closing formula of the fourth discourse, when Jesus had finished saying these things, and so begins the journey narrative that will carry the Gospel to Jerusalem. Chapters 19 and 20 run on a single thread, the question of what stands between a person and the kingdom, and they are framed by a saying about first and last that appears at the end of chapter 19, verse 30, and again at the end of the vineyard parable in 20:16. That inclusion makes the whole block one unit.

Inside the chapter the three scenes are tied by a deliberate contrast of stances. The Pharisees come to test Him, the disciples come to rebuke the children's bringers, and the young man comes to ask a question. Each has a hidden grip, on a legal loophole, on adult dignity, on possessions. Each scene is also a different kind of question, a legal one, a pastoral one, and a personal one, yet Jesus answers each by turning the questioner back to the beginning, to the Father's welcome, and to the One who is good.

Matthew shapes the divorce scene as a dispute story with a clear logic. The Pharisees raise a question about Moses' law, Jesus answers from creation in verses 4 to 6, they push back with Deuteronomy in verse 7, and Jesus distinguishes what Moses permitted from what God intended in verses 8 and 9. The disciples' reaction in verse 10 pushes the discussion into a second stage about who can receive the word. The rich young man scene is a miniature drama, with a question, a counter-question, a list, a claim, a further question and a tragic departure in verse 22. The last paragraph turns to the disciples and runs from astonishment to Peter's blunt question to a promise that has both a throne and a warning.
context.historical:
The scene opens in the region of Judea beyond the Jordan, which lay in the territory ruled by Herod Antipas, the same ruler who had John the Baptist killed after John denounced his marriage, Matthew 14:3-12. A question about divorce asked in that place was never a neutral classroom question, and it may have been meant to draw Jesus into the same dangerous territory.

The question of the Pharisees reflected a live debate. Deuteronomy 24:1 allows a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce if he finds some indecency in her, and the phrase was understood in different ways. A strict school restricted it to serious sexual misconduct, while a lax school allowed it for almost any displeasure. By asking whether divorce was lawful for any reason, they ask Jesus to take sides. In the ancient world a woman had very few rights, and a certificate protected her from claims that she was still bound to her husband. A man who sent his wife away could leave her without support.

Children occupied the lowest rung of the social ladder. They were brought to teachers for a blessing, and the laying on of hands for prayer is the same gesture used in blessing in Genesis 48:14. The disciples' attempt to shield Jesus from them follows a view that a teacher's time belongs to adults.

Wealth in the world of the first hearers was often taken as a sign of God's favour, as the language of blessing in Deuteronomy 28 and in Proverbs suggests. That is why the disciples are astonished at verse 25: if the man with every visible mark of blessing cannot enter, who can be saved? The camel was the largest animal familiar to them and the needle's eye the smallest opening, so the saying is deliberate exaggeration. A later story that the Needle's Eye was a small gate in Jerusalem lacks support in early sources and is better set aside.
context.canonical:
Jesus' answer on marriage is built from the first two chapters of the Bible. He joins Genesis 1:27, male and female He created them, with Genesis 2:24, a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh. The Pharisees had gone to Deuteronomy, Jesus goes behind it to creation. The same appeal to the beginning shapes Paul's teaching in Ephesians 5:31-32, where the one flesh union is a profound mystery that speaks of Christ and the church, and 1 Corinthians 7:10-16, where Paul reports the Lord's command and then applies it to a believer married to an unbeliever. Malachi 2:14-16 gives the prophetic background: the LORD was a witness to the covenant of marriage, and He hates divorce. Matthew 5:31-32 gives the earlier form of the exception clause.

The blessing of the children belongs with Matthew 18:1-5, where a child is the model of the kingdom, and with Mark 10:13-16 and Luke 18:15-17. The prophets' welcome of the outsider, as in Isaiah 56:3-5, provides the wider canon in which the least are brought in.

The rich man's story is told in all three Synoptic Gospels, Mark 10:17-31 and Luke 18:18-30, and the command to sell is paired with Jesus' similar teaching in Luke 12:33. The warnings against money are at the heart of Matthew 6:24, You cannot serve both God and money, and 1 Timothy 6:9-10 and 6:17-19 apply it to the church. The saying about what is impossible with man echoes Genesis 18:14 and Jeremiah 32:17, where nothing is too difficult for the LORD. The renewal of all things looks forward to Isaiah 65:17, Acts 3:21 and Revelation 21:5.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew gathers three conversations that look unrelated and shows that they have one theme, which is how the kingdom is received. A people formed by the Torah was used to asking what is permitted, what is required, what must I do. Jesus keeps moving the question from permission to purpose. On marriage He does not argue over the limits of a legal concession but recalls what God made in the beginning. On the children He says the kingdom is not earned but received. On the rich man He exposes that a person can keep every commandment on the surface and still be held by something else.

Matthew also wants the church to hear that Jesus' demands are real, because after verse 10 and verse 25 the disciples react with dismay. The reply in each case is not to soften the demand but to point to the grace that makes it possible: only those to whom it has been given, verse 11, and with God all things are possible, verse 26. The chapter finishes with a promise as large as the demand. Those who have left all will receive a hundredfold and eternal life, verse 29.

The warning at the end, many who are first will be last, is a sign that the first hearers could not rest on their status. Matthew writes to a church that includes people of great wealth and people of none, and the closing saying holds all of them under the same grace.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The teaching on marriage is prescriptive, because Jesus states what God joined and what a man must not separate, verse 6. It is given in the context of a debate and addresses the question the Pharisees asked, yet it is not a complete code for every hard case. Matthew's own version includes an exception, and Paul in 1 Corinthians 7 applies the principle to cases that the Gospel does not mention. The passage should be read with compassion for those who have been hurt, since Jesus' concern is to protect the vulnerable spouse and to honour the one flesh union, not to add burdens.

The saying about eunuchs in verse 12 describes three kinds of people who do not marry and does not command celibacy to everyone. It is addressed to those who can accept it.

The command to the rich young man is a specific word to a specific man, not a rule that every disciple must sell all. Zacchaeus gave half his goods and was declared saved, Luke 19:8-9, and Paul tells the wealthy to be generous and rich in good works, 1 Timothy 6:17-19. What does carry over is the test: Jesus names the thing the person cannot release. The command to follow Him is directed at every reader. The camel saying is hyperbole and is meant to be heard as such.

debates.question: What does the exception clause allow?

views.label: Divorce and remarriage after sexual unfaithfulness
views.case: The words except for sexual immorality are read as giving a ground on which the innocent party may divorce and marry again, since the marriage bond has already been broken. This is the view of most of the Reformation churches and many modern interpreters.

views.label: Divorce but not remarriage
views.case: Others say the exception allows separation or divorce but that the remarriage clause in the sentence refers to cases without the exception, so that the bond remains. This was common in the early church and is held in some Catholic and Orthodox traditions in different forms.

views.label: A reference to a specific kind of unlawful union
views.case: A third view reads porneia narrowly as referring to a marriage that was illegitimate from the start, for example within forbidden degrees, so that the clause permits ending a union that was never valid.

debates.bearing: The common ground is that Jesus calls marriage a lifelong union and that divorce is a concession to hardness of heart. The disagreement is over the exact reach of the exception, and the disagreement should be held with humility and with care for those in broken marriages.

debates.question: Is the command to sell everything for all believers?

views.label: A particular test for this man
views.case: Jesus puts His finger on this man's idol, his great wealth, verse 22. Others, like Zacchaeus, are told something different, and Luke 19:9 declares salvation to have come to a man who gave half his possessions.

views.label: A standard for the whole church
views.case: Some in the history of the church have taken the saying as a call to voluntary poverty for those who would be perfect, and Acts 4:32-35 shows believers holding things in common.

views.label: A demonstration that no one can keep the law to the full
views.case: The man claims to have kept the commandments and still lacks, which shows that even the best obedience falls short of the demand to love God above all, Deuteronomy 6:5. On this reading Jesus' answer drives him to the impossible and so to grace.

debates.bearing: Each reading contains something true. The word is aimed at one man's idol, it tests every hearer's relation to possessions, and it shows that the way into the kingdom is not law-keeping but following Jesus, which is a gift of God, verse 26.

debates.question: When is the renewal of all things?

views.label: At the return of Christ
views.case: Verse 28 places the renewal when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne, which fits Matthew 25:31 and the restoration of all things in Acts 3:21 and the new creation of Revelation 21:5.

views.label: Begun now and completed at the end
views.case: Others note that the new birth of the believer is also called renewal, Titus 3:5, and that the apostles' judging began with the founding of the church, with the final fulfilment awaiting the end.

debates.bearing: The text points to the final age, but the Bible sees that age breaking in through Christ's resurrection, so that those who follow Him already share in its firstfruits.

study.originalLanguages:
Two verbs in the divorce discussion carry weight. In verse 6 God has joined together, a verb that means to yoke together, from the picture of a pair of animals under one yoke. The union is described as God's doing, not just the couple's. The verb in verse 5 for being united means to be glued or joined fast. Together the two verbs describe a bond that is meant to be as permanent as a yoke and as close as a glued joint.

The Pharisees speak of Moses ordering a divorce certificate, entellomai, and Jesus corrects the verb: Moses permitted it, epitrepo. The law of Deuteronomy 24:1-4 regulated an existing practice and did not command it. Jesus gives the reason, hardness of heart, in Greek sklerokardia, a word that describes a heart that has set hard, close to the stubborn heart of Deuteronomy 10:16. He then adds that it was not so from the beginning, a phrase that sets creation above concession.

The exception clause turns on porneia, a broad word for sexual immorality of any kind. It occurs in Matthew 5:32 and in the list of evil things that come from the heart in Matthew 15:19, and in Acts 15:20 and 15:29 for the sexual sins the Gentile believers must avoid. A narrower verb, moichao, to commit adultery, is used in the same verse for what follows an illegitimate remarriage, which is part of why interpreters debate whether Jesus chose the broader word to include more than adultery. The BSB footnote notes that some manuscripts add a clause about marrying a divorced woman.

The word for the saying on accepting is choreo, to have room for, in verses 11 and 12. It speaks of a capacity given, and the verb dedotai, has been given, makes it a gift. Eunuch, eunouchos, is a person who does not marry, and Jesus lists three kinds, the born, the made and those who choose for the kingdom's sake.

In the rich man's story, the man asks what good thing he must do, using the verb poieo, to do, and Jesus answers by turning from the good thing to the One who is good, verse 17. The BSB footnote says some manuscripts read Why do you call Me good, as Mark 10:18 has it. Either way, Jesus moves the man's attention from deeds to God. The word teleios in verse 21 means complete, mature or whole, the same word used in Matthew 5:48 and in Deuteronomy 18:13 in the Greek, which says to be blameless before the LORD. Jesus is not describing an optional higher tier but wholeness, a heart with nothing held back.

Finally, palingenesia in verse 28 is a compound of palin, again, and genesis, beginning, a new birth or a beginning again. In the New Testament it appears only here and in Titus 3:5, where it describes the washing of new birth. The Greek word for hundredfold in verse 29 is a multiple, and the same verse adds eternal life, which is the real inheritance.

typology.type: Adam and Eve, the first one flesh union, Genesis 2:24
typology.fulfillment: The first marriage is a pattern as well as a precedent. Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and says the profound mystery is Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31-32. The husband gives himself for his wife as Christ gave Himself for the church, Ephesians 5:25. The escalation lies in the fact that marriage was always meant to point beyond itself to a covenant love that does not let go. The type falls short in that earthly marriage is for this age, since in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage, Matthew 22:30, and the union of Christ and His people is the reality to which it points.

typology.type: Abraham leaving his father's house, Genesis 12:1
typology.fulfillment: God told Abraham to leave his country and his father's household and go to a land that He would show him, and Abraham went. The rich young man is told to leave what he has and follow, and he goes away sad. Abraham's obedience is the pattern and the young man's refusal the contrast. Hebrews 11:8-10 says Abraham went out not knowing where he was going, looking for the city with foundations. The fulfilment is in Jesus, who left heaven's glory for our sake, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and who calls disciples to follow Him with the same trust. The type falls short because Abraham's call led to a land, and Jesus' call leads to Himself.

typology.type: The twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve thrones, verse 28
typology.fulfillment: Israel was formed around twelve tribes, and Jesus appointed twelve disciples to correspond. When He promises twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel, He treats the apostles as the foundation of the renewed people of God. Revelation 21:12-14 pictures the new Jerusalem with twelve gates named for the tribes and twelve foundations named for the apostles. The correspondence shows that the old and new people are one story. It falls short in that the apostles do not govern by their own right, since the throne is the Son of Man's and they sit by His grant, as Jesus says to the sons of Zebedee in Matthew 20:23.

typology.type: The blessing laid on a child, Genesis 48:14-16
typology.fulfillment: Jacob laid his hands on Ephraim and Manasseh and blessed them, putting the younger before the elder. In the same gesture, Jesus lays His hands on the children and blesses them, and His saying about first and last repeats the old pattern of reversal. Mark adds that He took them in His arms, Mark 10:16. The escalation is that the blessing is not an ancestral inheritance but the kingdom itself, for the kingdom belongs to such as these. The type falls short in that Jacob's blessing passed on a family promise, and Jesus' blessing welcomes those who have no family claim to give.

study.christ:
This chapter shows Jesus first as the One who speaks with the Creator's authority. When the Pharisees quote Moses, Jesus does not argue from a rival tradition. He says that the Creator made them male and female and said what a man will do, and He attributes the words of Genesis 2:24, which the narrator wrote, to God Himself. Then He says now I tell you, verse 9, which sets His own word beside Moses without apology. Hebrews 3:3-6 says that Jesus has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses, as a son over a house is greater than a servant in it.

He is the One in whom marriage finds its meaning. The one flesh of Genesis is the picture of a union that Paul says refers to Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:32. Jesus defends the marriage covenant because He is going to the cross to keep a covenant with a people who have been unfaithful. The divorcee, the abandoned spouse and the single are not left outside this picture, because Christ's faithfulness is greater than any human failing, and the single, in verse 12, serve the kingdom with undivided devotion, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 7:32-35.

He is the welcomer of the helpless. The disciples tried to protect His time, and Jesus said do not hinder them. A King who welcomes those who bring nothing is the King whose kingdom belongs to such as these, which fits His own invitation to the weary, Matthew 11:28-30.

He is the One who is good. The rich man called Him Teacher and asked about a good thing, and Jesus said there is only One who is good. This is not a denial of His own goodness, but a challenge to the man to see who he is speaking to. The man who is told to come, follow Me, is invited into the company of the One who is good. The sorrow with which the man leaves is the measure of what he refused: he walked away from the treasure, and the treasure was the person asking him to follow.

He is also the One who makes the impossible possible. The disciples ask who then can be saved, and the answer, with God all things are possible, is not an abstraction. It points to the cross in the next chapter, where the Son of Man gives His life as a ransom for many, Matthew 20:28. He is the One who has left everything, glory, riches and home, so that others might inherit eternal life.

Finally He is the King of the renewed world. He sits on His glorious throne, verse 28, and shares it with those who followed Him. Care is needed here not to turn the camel and the needle into a hidden picture of Christ. The Christological weight is carried by His authority, His welcome and His call, and by what He Himself says about what He will give.
study.god:
The God shown in this chapter is the Creator who made human beings male and female and who has a purpose for marriage. The words from the beginning say that He has not changed His mind. His design for marriage is rooted in the way He made the world, and He is the One who joins two people. Malachi says He is a witness at the wedding and hates the violence done in breaking faith, Malachi 2:14-16. The God of Matthew 19 is concerned for the wife who would be discarded, for the husband and wife who are to be one, and for the children who come from them.

He is also the God who does not let what He permits stand as what He wants. Moses' certificate was a concession, a mercy within a broken world, and Jesus is frank about it. God deals with human hardness by regulating it while keeping the original goal in sight. The same patience is shown in the whole of the Old Testament's law, which restrains harm without pretending to heal the heart.

God is the One who is good. Jesus' reply to the young man states a doctrine of God: goodness is not a human achievement to be measured by commandments, but a name for God Himself, and the one who wants to enter life must come to the One who is good. Psalm 62:10 and Matthew 6:24 show that the God who is good will not share His throne with money.

The chapter also shows a God who saves. With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible, verse 26. The line echoes Genesis 18:14 and Jeremiah 32:17, where nothing is too difficult for the LORD. Salvation is not a prize for the best but a work of the One who can do the impossible. Job 42:2 confesses that no plan of His can be thwarted.

The chapter holds together His demand and His generosity. He asks for everything and promises a hundredfold and eternal life. He tells the disciples that the first will be last, and the next chapter will show a landowner who pays all alike. The God of this passage is neither a harsh examiner nor an indulgent giver, but a Father who calls for undivided hearts and gives more than anyone can lose.

For worship the passage teaches us to come as children, empty handed, and to give up whatever stands between us and Him. We bring marriages, children, wealth and ambitions before the Creator, who made and owns them all, and we receive them back as His gifts.

crossReferences.note: The first half of Jesus' creation argument: God made them male and female. The Pharisees thought of marriage as a legal arrangement, and Jesus begins with what God made, the pairing of man and woman in the image of God.

A man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh. Jesus attributes these words to the Creator, and they give the basis for the statement that what God has joined, no one may separate.

The law of the certificate that the Pharisees quote. It describes what happens when a man finds some indecency in his wife and regulates the case, and it forbids him to remarry her after she has been married to another. Jesus reads it as a regulation of a concession and not an endorsement of divorce for any reason.

The LORD is a witness between a man and the wife of his youth, and says He hates divorce. The prophet's words show that God's concern for faithfulness in marriage is rooted in covenant, which is the background of Jesus' reply.
Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and says the mystery is about Christ and the church. It shows how Jesus' appeal to the beginning is taken up by the apostles, and why marriage is more than a human contract.

Paul applies the Lord's command that a wife must not separate from her husband and a husband must not divorce his wife, and then addresses the case of a believer married to an unbeliever. It shows the early church applying the principle with both firmness and pastoral care.

The earlier scene in which a child stands among the disciples as the model of the kingdom. The blessing of the children in 19:13-15 continues the same lesson and shows that the disciples had not yet understood it.
Mark's version of the rich man adds that Jesus looked at him and loved him, verse 21. The detail shows that the demand to sell all was spoken in love, not in judgment.

Zacchaeus, a rich man, gives half of his possessions to the poor and repays fourfold, and Jesus says salvation has come to his house. The contrast with the rich young man shows that wealth is not the real issue but the heart's hold on it.

No one can serve two masters, You cannot serve both God and money. The saying states in a sentence what the rich man's story shows in a scene, a heart divided between following Jesus and keeping a fortune.

Is anything too difficult for the LORD. The question put to Abraham when Sarah laughed lies behind Jesus' answer that with God all things are possible, and it shows that the impossible salvation is the same power that gave Isaac.

The only other New Testament use of the word for new birth that appears in Matthew 19:28. Paul uses it for the washing of new birth and renewal by the Spirit, linking the cosmic renewal of Jesus' saying with the personal renewal of each believer.

The One on the throne says Behold, I make all things new. It is the fulfilment of the renewal that Jesus promises the disciples when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne, and of the hope in Isaiah 65:17.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a marriage. Genesis 1 and 2 show God making humanity male and female, joining them, and setting them in a garden in which nothing stands between them and Him. The fall breaks the union at every level. Adam and Eve hide, then blame, and what had been one flesh becomes a quarrel, Genesis 3:12. Everything that Jesus says in Matthew 19 is shaped by that history. Divorce and its certificate belong to the world after the fall, a regulated concession to hard hearts, and Jesus' appeal to the beginning is a call to look at what God intended and to expect that He will restore it.

The chapter also touches the second great strand of the story, the question of who may enter. A young man with every advantage asks what he must do, and he is told that what he lacks is not one more deed but the One he is speaking to. The story of Israel is full of people who thought that they could earn their way, and of the God who said that He would give them a new heart. When the disciples ask who can be saved, the answer is the answer of the whole Bible: not by what man can do, but by what God can do.

It sets up what follows. The next chapter is the parable of the vineyard, in which a landowner pays all workers alike, and the third announcement of the cross, in which the One who tells the rich man to give everything gives His own life. The first will be last and the last first, because the King Himself became last, Matthew 20:28.

The story ends where the chapter points. There is a marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7, in which the union of Christ and His church is complete, and a throne on which the Son of Man sits and shares His reign. There is a renewed world, in which the One on the throne says all things are made new, Revelation 21:5. Those who left houses and family for His name receive more than they left, a family without grief, a treasure without moth, and life without end. The rich man's sorrow is answered at the last by the invitation he turned from, Come, follow Me.

quiz.q: On what basis does Jesus answer the question about divorce?

options.text: God's creation design: marriage is a lifelong one-flesh union that man must not separate.
options.note: Verses 4-6 appeal to creation, not merely to Moses' concession.

options.text: The certificate of divorce that Moses commanded.
options.note: Jesus addresses Moses' permission, but calls it a concession to hard hearts, not the original design.

options.text: Whatever the culture of the day found acceptable.
options.note: Jesus rejects the lax any-reason view, appealing to God's design instead.

options.text: A rule that divorce is always forbidden with no exception.
options.note: Jesus names a narrow exception; the point is God's design, not an absolute ban with no exception.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus welcome the little children?

options.text: Because the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who receive it like them.
options.note: Verse 14 makes the children a picture of childlike reception of the kingdom.

options.text: Because He wanted to bless as many people as possible.
options.note: He does bless them, but the reason given is that the kingdom belongs to such as these.

options.text: Because children had earned a place by their innocence.
options.note: The point is dependent reception, not earned merit or innocence.

options.text: Because the disciples had asked Him to bless them.
options.note: The disciples rebuked those bringing the children; Jesus overruled them.

quiz.q: Why did the rich young man go away sorrowful?

options.text: His wealth was the idol he would not surrender to follow Jesus.
options.note: Verses 21-22 expose his great wealth as the one thing he could not release.

options.text: Jesus asked more of him than of anyone else.
options.note: Jesus named his particular idol; the deeper issue is that his heart served wealth, not the size of the demand.

options.text: He had failed to keep any of the commandments.
options.note: He claimed to have kept them; his lack was an undivided heart, not total failure.

options.text: Jesus refused to tell him how to gain eternal life.
options.note: Jesus told him plainly; he refused the call, not the other way around.

quiz.q: What does Jesus teach about who can be saved?

options.text: Salvation is impossible for man but possible with God.
options.note: Verse 26 grounds salvation in God's power, not human ability.

options.text: Only the poor can be saved, not the rich.
options.note: Riches are a serious danger, but the point is that God can save even a rich person; salvation is God's work.

options.text: Anyone can save themselves by keeping the commandments.
options.note: The young man kept them outwardly yet lacked; salvation is God's doing, not self-achievement.

options.text: No one can ever be saved at all.
options.note: With God all things are possible; salvation is real, though only God can accomplish it.

quiz.q: What does Jesus promise those who leave everything to follow Him?

options.text: A hundredfold now and eternal life, sharing His reign in the renewal of all things.
options.note: Verses 28-29 promise abundant reward and a share in the coming renewal.

options.text: That they will avoid all hardship in this life.
options.note: Reward is promised, but not an escape from hardship; the reward includes the age to come.

options.text: That they have earned salvation by their sacrifice.
options.note: The reward is God's generous gift, not a wage earned; salvation remains His work.

options.text: Nothing, since following Jesus brings only loss.
options.note: Jesus explicitly promises a hundredfold and eternal life.

questions: Jesus rooted marriage in God's design from the beginning. How does seeing marriage as something God joins, rather than a contract we manage, shape the way you honor it?
The kingdom belongs to those who come like children. Where is adult self-sufficiency keeping you from receiving God's grace with open, empty hands?
Jesus named the one thing the young man could not release. What is the possession, comfort, or security you would find hardest to give up for Him?
Salvation is impossible for man but possible with God. How does that free you from both despair about others and pride about yourself?
Those who leave all for Christ receive a hundredfold. Where is fear of loss holding you back from a step of obedience He is asking?

translationNotes.note: Some manuscripts add and he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery, as in Matthew 5:32; the exception, except for sexual immorality, renders the Greek porneia, whose scope is discussed in the study.
Some manuscripts read Good Teacher and Why do you call Me good, as in Mark and Luke; the BSB follows the reading Why do you ask Me about what is good, with the same force, that God alone is good.
The word rendered the renewal of all things may also be translated the regeneration; it names the coming restoration of creation when the Son of Man reigns on His glorious throne.
